# 📥 Getting the data in {.subsection background-color="#425556"}

## Import: the first step of the pipeline

```{r, echo=FALSE, out.width="70%", fig.alt="The data science pipeline: import, then tidy, then a loop of transform, visualise and model, then communicate. The import step is highlighted: data import is the first step of the pipeline."}
knitr::include_graphics("images/fig-data-import.png")
```

::: {.content-visible unless-format="revealjs"}
In terms of the data science pipeline, every data science project starts with **getting the data into our software**. This step is called **data import**.
:::

## In this unit

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
How to get **tabular data** into R:

-   📄 **Delimited** text files: CSV, TSV, ...
-   📗 **Excel** workbooks
-   📊 Files from **statistical software**: SAS, SPSS, Stata

. . .

and the **arguments** that work around the usual caveats.

::: callout-note
## Disclaimer

Some data used in this unit is simulated.
:::

:::

::: {.content-visible unless-format="revealjs"}
In this unit, we show **how to get data into R**:

-   We consider **two particular cases**: *delimited* files and *MS Excel workbooks*. Both are examples of **tabular data**, i.e. data that comes in tables.
-   We touch upon some **caveats** and illustrate the **arguments** of the importing functions that allow us to work around them.
-   We also illustrate how to **import other file types**, namely files generated by statistical software.
:::

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
::: {.notes}
Ask participants whether they work (or will have to work) with Excel or SAS files. If not, don't go too much into the details of the Excel example.
:::
:::

# 📄 Delimited files {.subsection background-color="#425556"}

## A table in a text file

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}

Data entries are stored as a **table** in a **text file**.

-   One row of the table per line
-   Columns separated by a **delimiter** 

| separator | format  | extension |
|-----------|---------|-----------|
| comma `,` | **C**omma-**S**eparated **V**alues  | `.csv` |
| comma `,` | **C**omma-**S**eparated **V**alues  | `.csv` |
| semicolon `;` | **T**ab-**S**eparated **V**alues | `.tsv` |     

:::

::: {.content-visible unless-format="revealjs"}
In delimited files, the data entries are stored as a **table** in a **text file**. Columns are separated by a specific **delimiter character**, e.g. a comma (`,`), a semicolon (`;`) or a tabulation character (tab for short).

The delimiters give their **names** to the two most widespread file types: CSV (**C**omma-**S**eparated **V**alues) and TSV (**T**ab-**S**eparated **V**alues).
:::

## {.center}

```{r, echo=FALSE, out.width="70%", fig.alt="The same small table (name, gender, weight, height, bmi) saved in two text formats: team.csv, where the values are separated by commas, and team.tsv, where they are separated by tabs."}
knitr::include_graphics("images/1-delim.png")
```

## CSV is the most common format for sharing data

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}

::: {.incremental}
-   Small- and mid-sized data, up to several GB
-   **Software-agnostic**: any tool can open it
-   Especially important when you **work in a team**!
:::
:::

::: {.content-visible unless-format="revealjs"}
CSV files are the **most common file format for sharing small- and mid-sized data** (up to several GB). Their main advantage is that they are **software-agnostic**: any program can read them. This is especially important if you work in a team!
:::

## `read_csv()` reads a CSV file into R

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
-   From `{readr}`, part of the `{tidyverse}`
-   Give it the **path to the file**, on your computer or on the web
-   **Store the result** in an object
:::

::: {.content-visible unless-format="revealjs"}
R has dozens of functions to import such files. We use the functions of the `{readr}` package, which is part of the `{tidyverse}`. The function `read_csv()` reads CSV files.

We need to give it the **path to the file**, on our computer or even on the web. It is convenient to **store the data in an object**, so we can use it later on:
:::

```{r, eval = FALSE}
name_of_object <- read_csv("path_to_file")
```

## Example: reading `team.csv`

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
👉 First, open `data/team.csv` and have a look at it.
:::

::: {.content-visible unless-format="revealjs"}
A file called `team.csv` is in the folder `data`. Inspect it by opening it first. In our case, the path to give to `read_csv()` is `"data/team.csv"`.
:::

```{r}
library(readr)

team <- read_csv("data/team.csv")
```

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
. . .
:::

```{r}
team
```

## Use paths *relative* to your document

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
-   ✅ `"data/team.csv"`
-   ❌ `"/Users/jack/Documents/my/unique/folders/data/team.csv"`

. . .

-   Relative paths work on **any computer**: share the folder as it is
-   In Quarto / R Markdown, they start from the **document's folder**
:::

::: {.content-visible unless-format="revealjs"}
Quarto and R Markdown documents work with **relative** paths, which makes writing file paths easier.

-   Our document lies in a folder that contains a `data` folder, where the file `team.csv` is found.
-   So the path to `team.csv` can be written **relative to the position of the document**, i.e. `"data/team.csv"`, as opposed to an absolute path such as `"/Users/jack/Documents/my/unique/folders/data/team.csv"`.
-   This is extremely beneficial, especially if you're **working with a collaborator!** The same code runs on their computer, whatever their folder structure.

:::{.callout-warning}

Paths start from the document's folder **only in Quarto / R Markdown documents**. In R scripts and in the console, they start from the *working directory* instead.
:::

:::

## Useful arguments of `read_csv()`

```{r, echo=FALSE, out.width="80%", fig.alt="A call to read_csv() with the arguments file, col_names, na and skip, each linked by an arrow to what it controls in a CSV file: the file name, the header row with the column names, the 'null' values to treat as missing, and the three lines of notes above the data to skip."}
knitr::include_graphics("images/1-read_csv.png")
```

::: callout-tip
::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
Forgot an argument's name? Put the cursor inside the parentheses and press <kbd>Tab</kbd>.
:::

::: {.content-visible unless-format="revealjs"}
If you don't remember the exact name of an argument, move your cursor inside the parentheses and hit <kbd>Tab</kbd>. The function's argument list pops up: you can select the one you need and even read a short description.
:::
:::

## `col_names = FALSE`: the first row is data {.smaller}

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
-   By default, `read_csv()` takes **the first row** as the **column names**
-   No header in the file? Set `col_names = FALSE`: R names the columns `X1`, `X2`, ...
:::

::: {.content-visible unless-format="revealjs"}
By default, `read_csv()` considers **the first row** as the **column names**. However, sometimes the file's **first row is data**. The argument `col_names` defines **how to treat the first row**: if it does not contain the column names, we set `col_names = FALSE`, and R generates the column names `X1`, `X2`, etc.

The file `team_wo_header.csv` does not have a header:
:::

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="40%"}
```{r, comment=NA, echo=FALSE}
cat(read_lines("data/team_wo_header.csv", n_max = 4), sep = "\n")
```
:::

::: {.column width="60%"}
```{r}
team_wo_header <-
  read_csv(
    "data/team_wo_header.csv",
    col_names = FALSE)

team_wo_header
```
:::
::::

## `na = "null"`: declare the missing values {.smaller}

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
-   R writes missing values as `NA`, other programs write e.g. `null`
-   `read_csv()` reads `null` as text, so **whole columns become text**
:::

::: {.content-visible unless-format="revealjs"}
In R, **missing values are denoted as `NA`**. However, other programs have other ways of declaring a missing value, e.g. `null`. When imported with `read_csv()`, these are read as the **character string `"null"`**, and every column that contains one is imported as characters, even if it holds numbers.

Take a look at the `team_missing.csv` dataset:
:::

```{r, comment=NA, echo=FALSE}
cat(read_lines("data/team_missing.csv", n_max = 4), sep = "\n")
```

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
team_missing <- read_csv("data/team_missing.csv")
team_missing
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
team_missing <- read_csv("data/team_missing.csv", na = "null")
team_missing
```
:::
::::

::: {.content-visible unless-format="revealjs"}
Setting `na = "null"` is a lifesaver in this case: the numeric columns are numbers again.
:::

## `skip = 3`: jump over the metadata {.smaller}

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
-   Some text files start with a **description of the data** (metadata)
-   `skip` tells `read_csv()` how many lines to jump over
:::

::: {.content-visible unless-format="revealjs"}
CSV files are text files, so they are sometimes stored as `.txt`. Some text files have a **description of the data in their first lines**, sometimes called "metadata". When importing the data into a tibble, **these lines must be skipped**, which can be done with the argument `skip`.

The file `team_meta.txt` starts with three lines of metadata:
:::

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="45%"}
```{r, comment=NA, echo=FALSE}
cat(read_lines("data/team_meta.txt", n_max = 7), sep = "\n")
```
:::

::: {.column width="55%"}
```{r}
team_meta <- read_csv("data/team_meta.txt", skip = 3)
team_meta
```
:::
::::

## `locale`: special characters {.smaller}

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
-   Accents and umlauts (French, German, ...) can come out garbled
-   Tell `read_csv()` the file's **encoding**: `locale = locale(encoding = "latin1")`
:::

::: {.content-visible unless-format="revealjs"}
The argument `locale` helps you avoid encoding issues. It is especially useful when a CSV file is in a **language with special characters** (e.g. French, German, etc.). Setting `locale = locale(encoding = "latin1")` reads the file with the `latin1` encoding, so the special characters are imported correctly.

Compare the output of the following code chunks:
:::

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
#| error: true
cities <- read_csv("data/cities.csv")
cities
```
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
```{r}
cities <- read_csv(
  "data/cities.csv",
  locale = locale(encoding = "latin1"))
cities
```
:::
::::

## Other delimiters, same arguments

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
-   Countries with a **decimal comma** use `;` as a delimiter → `read_csv2()`
-   Tabs → `read_tsv()`, any other delimiter → `read_delim()`
-   They all take the **same arguments** as `read_csv()`
:::

::: {.content-visible unless-format="revealjs"}
Since `read_csv()` uses a comma (`,`) as a delimiter, it assumes that the **decimal mark is a dot (`.`)**. Otherwise, it would confuse decimal marks with separators!

-   In countries that use a **decimal comma**, the **delimiter is typically a semicolon (`;`)**. `read_csv()` has a twin sibling for these files: `read_csv2()`.
-   Two other functions, `read_tsv()` and `read_delim()`, read tab-separated files and files with any other delimiter.
-   Another nicety of `{readr}`: all the arguments we've seen are available in these functions too.

The table below summarises the `{readr}` functions and their delimiters.
:::

```{r, echo=FALSE}
tribble(
  ~ `Function`, ~ `Delimiter`, ~ `Default decimal`,
  "`read_csv()`", "`,` (comma)", "`.` (dot)",
  "`read_csv2()`", "`;` (semicolon)", "`,` (comma)",
  "`read_tsv()`", "Tab", "`.` (dot)",
  "`read_delim()`", "Custom", "`.` (dot)",
) %>%
  knitr::kable()
```

# 📗 Excel files {.subsection background-color="#425556"}

## `{readxl}` reads Excel workbooks

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
-   Installed with the `{tidyverse}`, but **not attached** by `library(tidyverse)`
-   `read_xls()` for `.xls`, `read_xlsx()` for `.xlsx`, `read_excel()` guesses
-   First argument: the **path** to the file
:::

::: {.content-visible unless-format="revealjs"}
MS Excel is one of the most popular formats for storing small datasets, so let's see **how to import data from Excel files**, usually with an `.xls` or `.xlsx` extension.

We use the `{readxl}` package. It is installed along with the `{tidyverse}`, but it is not part of its core, so `library(tidyverse)` doesn't attach it. If it is missing on your system, install it:
:::

``` r
install.packages("readxl")
```

::: callout-warning
## Note

You don't have to do this on Renku, as it has been installed already!
:::

::: {.content-visible unless-format="revealjs"}
Once it is installed, we attach it. To read data from Excel into R, `{readxl}` has several functions: `read_xls()` for `.xls` files, `read_xlsx()` for `.xlsx` files, and `read_excel()`, which guesses the file format automatically. As with `{readr}`, the **first argument** is the **path** to the file.
:::

```{r}
library(readxl)
```

## Example: reading `team.xlsx`

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
👉 First, open `data/team.xlsx` in Excel and look at how it is structured.
:::

::: {.content-visible unless-format="revealjs"}
Open the file `team.xlsx` (with MS Excel) and have a look at how it is structured. Then, let's import it into R and store its contents in the object `team`:
:::

```{r}
team <- read_xlsx("data/team.xlsx")
team
```

## Excel files can be a mess!

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
👉 Open `data/je-e-06.02.00.01.02.xlsx`:

-   A **workbook** with several **sheets**
-   The table sits somewhere in the middle of the cells
:::

::: {.content-visible unless-format="revealjs"}
Excel files are not always clean and tidy. For instance, check the file `je-e-06.02.00.01.02.xlsx`: it's an **Excel workbook** with several **sheets**, and the data is spread over many **cells**. By the end of this section, you'll be able to get the data you need from this file. These are the arguments we use:
:::

```{r, echo=FALSE, out.width="70%", fig.alt="A call to read_excel() with the arguments file, sheet, range and col_names, each linked by an arrow to what it controls in an Excel workbook: the file name, the second sheet, the cell range C3:G23 that holds the table, and its header row."}
knitr::include_graphics("images/2-excel.png")
```

## `sheet`: which sheet to import {.smaller}

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
-   By **name**: `sheet = "Women"`, or by **position**: `sheet = 2`
-   Default: the **first** sheet
:::

::: {.content-visible unless-format="revealjs"}
An Excel file can have several sheets. The argument **`sheet`** controls **which sheet is imported**. It can be given as the **name of the sheet**, e.g. `sheet = "Women"`, or as **its position** in the workbook, e.g. `sheet = 2`. By default, `read_xlsx()` imports the **first sheet**.

Let's import the sheet `"Women"` from `je-e-06.02.00.01.02.xlsx`:
:::

```{r}
women_jobs <- read_xlsx(
  "data/je-e-06.02.00.01.02.xlsx",
  sheet = "Women"
)

women_jobs
```

::: callout-important
## Note

The data has been imported, but it isn't usable yet.
:::

## `range`: which cells to import {.smaller}

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
-   The data is all over the sheet: `skip` isn't enough
-   `range` takes the **upper-left** and **lower-right** cells: `range = "A9:DP72"`
:::

::: {.content-visible unless-format="revealjs"}
Specifying the `sheet` is not enough here, because the **data is all over the place** in the sheet, and skipping lines (with `skip`) wouldn't help. With the argument `range`, we refer to a **rectangle of cells** by its upper-left and lower-right cells, separated by a colon (`:`). For instance, `range = "B2:K14"` imports the data in the rectangle between cells B2 and K14.

In our file, the table lies between the cells A9 and DP72:
:::

```{r}
women_jobs <- read_xlsx(
  "data/je-e-06.02.00.01.02.xlsx",
  sheet = "Women",
  range = "A9:DP72"
)

women_jobs
```

## `col_names = FALSE`, again {.smaller}

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
-   Almost there, but the **column names contain values**
-   Same fix as for CSV files
:::

::: {.content-visible unless-format="revealjs"}
We are one step closer, but the **column names contain values**. The last step is to set an argument we already know: `col_names = FALSE`.
:::

```{r}
women_jobs <- read_xlsx(
  "data/je-e-06.02.00.01.02.xlsx",
  sheet = "Women",
  range = "A9:DP72",
  col_names = FALSE
)

women_jobs
```

# 📊 Files from statistical software {.subsection background-color="#425556"}

## `{haven}` reads SAS, SPSS and Stata files

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
-   One function per file type: `read_sas()`, `read_sav()`, `read_dta()`, ...
:::

::: {.content-visible unless-format="revealjs"}
Data might also come in a file format generated by statistical software, e.g. SAS, SPSS or Stata. Data from these programs can be imported with the `{haven}` package, which reads and writes `.sas7bdat`, `.sas7bcat`, `.xpt`, `.sav`, `.por` and `.dta` files.

The table below summarises which function to use:

```{r, echo=FALSE}
tribble(
  ~ `File extension`, ~ `Software`, ~ `Function`,
  "`.sas7bdat`", "SAS", "`read_sas()`",
  "`.sas7bcat`", "SAS", "`read_sas()`",
  "`.xpt`", "SAS", "`read_xpt()`",
  "`.sav`", "SPSS", "`read_sav()`",
  "`.por`", "SPSS", "`read_por()`",
  "`.dta`", "Stata", "`read_dta()`"
) %>%
  knitr::kable()
```
:::

```{r, echo=FALSE, out.width="70%", fig.alt="The {haven} package imports files from statistical software into R: read_sas() and read_xpt() for SAS, read_dta() for Stata, read_sav() and read_por() for SPSS."}
knitr::include_graphics("images/3-other.png")
```

## Example: reading a SAS file {.smaller}

::: {.content-visible unless-format="revealjs"}
For instance, let's import a SAS data file with `read_sas()`:
:::

```{r}
library(haven)

mtcars_data <- read_sas("data/mtcars.sas7bdat")

mtcars_data
```

::: {.content-visible when-format="revealjs"}
More arguments? See the documentation: `?read_sas`
:::

::: {.content-visible unless-format="revealjs"}
Since these file types are very specific, we won't cover each and every argument. However, you can always read the documentation, e.g. `?read_sas`!
:::
